curves.name: Pacific Northwest fire-killed mixed-conifer salvage volume retention
curves.retention_definition: Net recoverable volume relative to pre-disturbance green volume. Published as a net volume discount factor, not a lumber grade or price index.

source.citation: Prestemon, J.P. and Holmes, T.P. (2008). Timber Salvage Economics. In: Holmes, T.P., Prestemon, J.P., Abt, K.L. (eds) The Economics of Forest Disturbances. Springer, Dordrecht, pp. 167-190, section 4.2.6.
source.boundary: Weighted-average net volume discount factors for mixed-conifer fire-killed timber in southwest Oregon (Biscuit fire), derived from Lowell and Cahill (1996) and Prestemon et al. (2006). This is a reference curve, not a BC-specific, species-specific, or roadside-storage-specific operational curve.

product_windows.note: Most suitable time to salvage trees killed by spruce budworm or fire for lumber is generally limited to 1-2 years after death.

source.citation: Barrette, J., Thiffault, E., Saint-Pierre, F., Wetzel, S., Duchesne, I. and Krigstin, S. (2015). Dynamics of dead tree degradation and shelf-life following natural disturbances: can salvaged trees from boreal forests 'fuel' the forestry and bioenergy sectors? Forestry 88(3):275-290.
source.boundary: Canadian boreal review; product windows are advisory generalizations, not a mill-acceptance rule or a species-specific guarantee.

product_windows.note: Trees can usually be salvaged for pulp while wood moisture remains above fibre saturation, but salvage is usually not recommended after 3-4 years following death.

source.citation: Barrette, J., Thiffault, E., Saint-Pierre, F., Wetzel, S., Duchesne, I. and Krigstin, S. (2015). Dynamics of dead tree degradation and shelf-life following natural disturbances: can salvaged trees from boreal forests 'fuel' the forestry and bioenergy sectors? Forestry 88(3):275-290.
source.boundary: Canadian boreal review; product windows are advisory generalizations, not a mill-acceptance rule or a species-specific guarantee.

product_windows.note: Past the pulp window, salvaged trees may yield better opportunities for the bioenergy sector.
